extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants (PD/PIs), Authorized Organization Representatives (AORs), institutional grants administrators, and NIH peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_short: nih grant peer review and compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluation criteria governing NIH grant applications, peer review (initial and Council levels), confidentiality/FOIA/privacy matters, data release, and applicant recourse (appeals/resubmissions). Useful for applicants preparing submissions and reviewers conducting evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Most grant-related information submitted to NIH by the applicant or recipient in the application or in the post-award phase is considered public information and, once an award is made, is subject to possible release to individuals or organizations outside NIH. NIH routinely places information about awarded grants, including project title, the name of the PD/PI, and the project description, on the RePORT Web site. For funded research grant applications, NIH also sends the project description provided by an applicant to the DoC’s NTIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be aware that, except for certain proprietary or private information, application materials and award information can become public. Several policies require acknowledgment of support and disclaimers for publications, inventions, and other research products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of Information (proprietary submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are discouraged from submitting information considered proprietary unless it is deemed essential for proper evaluation of the application. If the application contains trade secrets, commercial or financial information, or privileged/confidential information, the pages containing that information should be identified as specified in the application instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proprietary information is included, it is furnished in confidence for evaluation and will be protected from unauthorized disclosure consistent with peer review needs and FOIA/Privacy Act requirements. Applicants must identify proprietary information at submission; failure to do so makes withholding under FOIA difficult. If notified after a FOIA request, the PD/PI will be given five (5) working days to identify potentially patentable or commercially valuable information with a specific description of commercial harm; vague claims will not be honored. Documents with both disclosable and non-disclosable information will be redacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Act protections for individual records
rubrics_metrics.description: The Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. 552a) provides safeguards for information about individuals maintained in a system of records, including rights to know what information is maintained, how it is used, how to access records, and how to correct or request deletion of factually incorrect information. NIH maintains application and grant records as a system of records (NIH 09-25-0225).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for release of Privacy Act records are processed under FOIA. NIH balances individual privacy rights with the public’s right to know when releasing information about an individual to a third party.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA: Types of records NIH generally will release
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH generally will release certain types of records pursuant to a FOIA request, including: funded applications and funded progress reports (including award data), and final reports transmitted to the recipient organization of any audit, survey, review, or evaluation of recipient performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other releases are handled case-by-case and applicants will be notified if NIH believes requested information could be exempt from release.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA: Types of records NIH generally will withhold
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH generally will withhold: pending competing grant applications; unfunded new, renewal, and revision applications; financial information pertaining to project personnel such as institutional base salary; information whose disclosure would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy; predecisional opinions in interagency/intraagency memoranda; evaluative portions of site visit reports and peer review summary statements, including impact scores; trade secrets and commercial/financial information privileged or confidential; information which if released would adversely affect the competitive position of the person/organization; patent or other valuable commercial rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must specifically identify proprietary material during submission. NIH FOI Officer has authority to deny requests and denials may be appealed to HHS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of Research Data (definition and coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research data are the recorded factual material commonly accepted in the scientific community as necessary to validate research findings. This does not include preliminary analyses, drafts, plans for future research, peer reviews, communications, physical objects, trade secrets, information necessary to be held confidential until publication, protected information (e.g., IP), or personally identifying/medical files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 2 CFR Part 200.315, institutions of higher education, hospitals, or non-profit organizations must release research data first produced in a federally funded project if the data are cited publicly and officially by a Federal agency in support of an action that has the force and effect of law (e.g., regulations/administrative orders). If data are publicly available, NIH will direct requesters to the public source; otherwise, IC FOI coordinator handles requests in consultation with affected recipient and PD/PI. Fees to cover recipient and NIH response costs may be assessed. The requirement does not apply to for-profit organizations or data produced by State/local governments unless contracted to an eligible institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting Sensitive Data and Information Used in Research
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must protect sensitive and confidential data as part of stewardship of federally funded research and take reasonable cybersecurity and other actions to prevent inadvertent disclosure or loss of sensitive personal information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH advises not to house personally identifiable, sensitive, or confidential information on portable electronic devices; if used, devices should be encrypted. Limit access with proper controls (passwords). Transmit research data only when the recipient’s systems security is known and satisfactory. See also FISMA requirements in Public Policy Requirements and Objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Review responsibilities (DRR/CSR/SRO/Reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Division of Receipt and Referral (DRR) receives all competing grant applications. CSR centrally reviews applications for completeness and responsiveness to the NOFO, conducts initial technical review for scientific merit, and prepares summary statements. CSR Referral Officers assign applications to ICs and to specific study sections for initial review based on contents and referral guidelines. SROs review applications for completeness and administrative conformity and assign at least three reviewers to write critiques, provide initial scores, and be prepared to discuss the applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRGs are primarily composed of non-federal scientists actively engaged in research. Ad hoc SEPs may be used when special expertise is required. NIH conflict-of-interest and confidentiality requirements apply. Applicants are notified of receipts and assignments via eRA Commons and may request reconsideration of SRG/IC assignment. SRO (not PO) is the primary contact until summary statement release. Applicants may withdraw applications any time; withdrawals must be signed by PD/PI and AOR and submitted to SRO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess overall impact to determine scientific and technical merit. For research grants and cooperative agreements, reviewers provide an overall impact score reflecting their assessment of the likelihood for the project to exert a sustained, powerful influence on the research field(s) involved, in consideration of the five scored review criteria and additional review criteria as applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria are evaluated and scored in accordance with the applicable peer review framework (standard or Simplified Review Framework (SRF)). An application does not need to be strong in all categories to be judged likely to have major scientific impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance (scored review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Significance — one of five regulatory criteria used to determine scientific and technical merit for research grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For non-SRF activity codes reviewers will determine a separate score for Significance. The NOFO should be consulted for additional information describing the criterion. An application need not be strong in every category to have major impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator(s) (scored review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigator(s) — one of five regulatory criteria used to determine scientific and technical merit for research grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers evaluate the qualifications, expertise, and appropriateness of the PD/PI and key personnel. For non-SRF activity codes reviewers will determine a separate score. NOFOs may provide further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation (scored review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation — one of five regulatory criteria used to determine scientific and technical merit for research grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assess whether the application uses novel concepts or approaches. For non-SRF activity codes reviewers will determine a separate score. NOFOs may provide further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach (scored review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach — one of five regulatory criteria used to determine scientific and technical merit for research grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers evaluate the rigor, feasibility, and appropriateness of the proposed methods. For non-SRF activity codes reviewers will determine a separate score. NOFOs may provide further detail; Approach may include human subjects protections, inclusion plans, and clinical trial timelines as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environment (scored review criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Environment — one of five regulatory criteria used to determine scientific and technical merit for research grant applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers consider institutional support, equipment, and other physical/environmental resources. For non-SRF activity codes reviewers will determine a separate score. NOFOs may provide further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Additional Review Criteria (non-SRF)
rubrics_metrics.description: As applicable, reviewers will consider additional items in the determination of scientific and technical merit and in providing an overall impact score, but will not give separate scores for these items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items include Protections for Human Subjects, Inclusion of Human Subjects, Vertebrate Animals, Biohazards, and Resubmission/Renewal/Revision Applications. Consult the NOFO for details on applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Additional Review Considerations (non-SRF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain items will be considered as part of review but should not be given scores or considered in providing an overall impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These considerations include Provision of Family Care Facilities (for Conference Grant Applications), Select Agent Research, Resource Sharing Plans, Authentication of Key Biological and/or Chemical Resources, and Budget and Period of Support. The NOFO should be consulted for further information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified Review Framework (SRF) overview
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH uses the Simplified Review Framework (SRF) for the peer review of the majority of competing research project grants under specified activity codes. SRF focuses reviewers on: the importance of the proposed research, whether the proposed research methods are rigorous and feasible, and whether the investigators and institution have the expertise and resources necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRF aims to mitigate reputational bias by refocusing investigator/environment evaluation within the context of the proposed research and reducing reviewer burden by shifting policy compliance activities to NIH staff. SRF reorganizes the five regulatory criteria into three factors; Factors 1 and 2 receive separate scores (1-9) and Factor 3 is evaluated for sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRF Factor 1: Importance of the Research (scored 1-9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor 1 comprises Significance and Innovation and is scored 1-9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers evaluate whether the research is important and innovative. An application does not need to be strong in all categories to be judged likely to have major scientific impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRF Factor 2: Rigor and Feasibility (scored 1-9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor 2 comprises Approach (and also includes Inclusion and Clinical Trial Study Timeline) and is scored 1-9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers assess the rigor, feasibility, and appropriateness of methods and timelines. Inclusion and clinical trial timelines are considered part of Approach under SRF.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRF Factor 3: Expertise and Resources (evaluated for sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor 3 comprises Investigator(s) and Environment and is evaluated for sufficiency rather than given a numeric score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigator(s) and Environment are evaluated as 'appropriate' or 'gaps identified'. If gaps are identified, the reviewer is required to provide further explanation. This evaluation is considered within the overall impact determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: SRF Additional Review Criteria and Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under SRF, certain additional items may affect the overall impact score but are not given separate scores, and some are explicitly not to be considered in providing the overall impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SRF Additional Review Criteria (can affect overall impact score) include Protections for Human Subjects, Vertebrate Animals, Biohazards, and Resubmission/Renewal/Revision Applications. SRF Additional Review Considerations (no effect on overall impact score) include Authentication of Key Biological/Chemical Resources and Budget and Period of Support. Consult the NOFO for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals of Initial Scientific Review (grounds and procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal is a written communication from a PD/PI and/or applicant institution that: is received after issuance of the summary statement and up to 30 calendar days after the second level of peer review; describes a flaw in the review process for a particular application; is based on one or more allowable issues; and displays concurrence from the AOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowable issues are: evidence of bias by one or more peer reviewers; conflict of interest as specified in 42 CFR Part 52h.5 for non-federal reviewers; lack of appropriate expertise within the SRG; and factual error(s) made by one or more reviewers that could have substantially altered the outcome. Appeals based solely on differences of scientific opinion are not accepted. The PD/PI should first contact the Program Official (PO) to discuss concerns. The appeal letter must include AOR concurrence (sent directly by AOR). NIH will acknowledge receipt within 10 days. If unresolved, the appeal may be made available to Council; Council may recommend re-review or deny the appeal. If re-review is recommended, the original application will be re-reviewed without additional materials. The Council recommendation is final.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Advisory Council/Board second-level review
rubrics_metrics.description: The IC National Advisory Council or Board provides the second level peer review, reviewing the summary statement and asked to concur with the SRG's initial peer review and to consider relevance to the IC's programs and priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Council members include senior scientists and public members. Council may concur, may decide not to recommend based on program/policy, or may defer and refer back to the SRG for re-review. With very limited exception, an application may not be considered for funding unless it has received a favorable recommendation by both the SRG and the Council. Applications from PD/PIs with $2M+ total NIH support may be identified for Special Council Review to consider unique opportunities. Council decisions are communicated in writing; if Council recommends re-review, re-review outcome is final and not appealable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of Applications and Resubmission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Incomplete, non-compliant, and nonresponsive applications will not be reviewed. If the NOFO remains open, the applicant may resubmit a corrected or complete investigator-initiated application for the next review cycle. One resubmission application may be submitted for an appropriate due date up to 37 months after the initial application due date; resubmissions after 37 months must be formatted and submitted as new applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complete and compliant applications, the summary statement will be available through eRA Commons to the PD/PI and AORs with the Signing Official role. Applicants receiving summary statements should consult NIH Next Steps guidance. If an application is unsuccessful, an applicant may submit one revised resubmission if the NOFO permits. IC Directors make final award decisions from among those applications receiving favorable initial review and Council recommendation. Some ICs publish paylines to guide applicants; scores should be compared against the payline for the fiscal year when the application will be considered for funding. Unsuccessful applicants receive centralized automated notification.
